                                               On permutation characters of finite groups

                                                                          Jiakuan Lu
                                                School of Mathematics and Statistics, Guangxi Normal University,
                                                              Guilin 541006, Guangxi, P. R. China
arXiv:2511.20171v1 [math.GR] 25 Nov 2025




                                                                               Abstract
                                                     Let G be a finite group and M be a maximal subgroup of G. We
                                                 call every irreducible constituent χ of (1M )G a P-character of G with
                                                 respect to M . In this paper, we prove that if all P-characters of G are
                                                 monomial, then G is solvable, which solves a question posed by Qian
                                                 and Yang.

                                               Keywords: P-characters; Solvable groups.
                                               MSC(2020): 20C15, 20D10


                                           1     Introduction
                                           Throughout this paper, G always denotes a finite group, p is a prime and
                                           π is a set of some primes. As usual, let Irr(G) be the set of all irreducible
                                           complex characters of G and cd(G) = {χ(1) | χ ∈ Irr(G)}. It is well-know
                                           that the structure of G is heavily determined by cd(G), and there are a lot
                                           of classical theorems on this subject. For example, see [1, 3].
                                               Recall that χ ∈ Irr(G) is monomial if χ is induced from a linear character
                                           of a subgroup of G, and that G is an M -group if all its irreducible characters
                                           are monomial. We know that M -groups are solvable and that every solvable
                                           group is contained in an M -group. More interesting results on M -groups can
                                           be found in [2].
                                               Let M be a maximal subgroup of G. Then G acts on the set of right cosets
                                           of M and it induces a transitive permutation character (1M )G . Let χ be an
                                           irreducible constituent of (1M )G . Followed by [4], we call χ a P-character of
                                           G with respect to M , and denote by IrrP (G) the set of P-characters of G and
                                           cdP (G) = {χ(1) | χ ∈ IrrP (G)}. If in addition |G : M | is a π-number where
                                           π is a set of primes, then χ is called a Pπ -character. Let IrrPπ (G) be the set
                                           of Pπ -characters of G. Clearly, if χ is a P-character of a solvable group, then
                                           χ is a Pp -character for some prime p. Moreover, a P-character of a solvable
                                           group is monomial and monolithic (see [4, Proposition 2.3]).
                                               In [4], the authors posed several questions, one of which is whether G is
                                           solvable if all P-characters of G are monomial. In the following theorem, we
                                           give an affirmative answer.

                                                                                    1
Theorem A. Let G be a group and assume that all P-characters of G are
monomial. Then G is solvable.

    In the following theorem, we prove a π-variation of [4, Proposition 2.5].

Theorem B. Let G be a π-solvable group. Then all Pπ -character degrees of
G are π-number if and only if G has a normal π-complement.

Theorem C. Let G be π-separable. If all members of Irr(G) are Pπ -characters,
then G is a π-group.

    Theorem C suggests that perhaps if G is a π-group, then IrrP (G) =
Irr(G). However, this is false in general. An easy counterexample in a solv-
able group is to take G to be SL(2, 3) and π = {2, 3}. Then the irreducible
characters of degree 2 of G are not P-characters.
    Note also that if IrrP (G) = Irr(G), then G is not necessarily solvable. As
pointed out by G. Navarro, PSL(2, 27) is such an example.
    By Corollary 2.6 of [4], a finite group G is nilpotent if and only if cdP (G) =
{1}. Let G = A5 , the alternating group of degree 5. Then cdP (G) = {1, 4, 5}.
After checking many examples, it seems reasonable to conjecture that if
|cdP (G)| ≤ 2, then G is solvable. In this paper, however, we cannot yet
prove it.


2     Proofs
Proof of Theorem A. Suppose the theorem does not hold, and let G be a
counterexample of minimal order.
    We first show that G is not a non-abelian simple group. Assuming that
this result false, we derive a contradiction. Let K be a proper subgroup of
G with the largest possible order. Then K is a maximal subgroup of G. Let
φ be a nonprincipal P-character of G with respect to K. Note that such φ
really exists by Frobenius Reciprocity. By assumption, φ is monomial, so we
may assume that φ = λG , where λ is a linear character of some subgroup K1
of G. Since

                (1K )G (1) = |G : K| ≥ 1 + φ(1) = 1 + |G : K1 |,

we must have that |K1 | > |K| and so K1 = G. It follows that φ is a
nonprincipal linear character of G and thus |G : G′ | ≥ 2, a contradiction.
    Let N be a minimal normal subgroup of G. Then N < G. Let χ ∈
Irr(G/N ) be a P-character of G/N with respect to the maximal subgroup
M/N . Then χ ∈ Irr(G) be a P-character of G with respect to the maximal

                                        2
subgroup M . By assumption, χ = η G , where
                                        T η is a xlinear character of some
subgroup M1 of G. Then N ≤ ker χ =         (ker η) ≤ ker η ≤ M1 . Thus,
                                            x∈G
χ ∈ Irr(G/N ) is monomial. By induction hypothesis, G/N is solvable. Then
N is not solvable. Clearly, N is the unique minimal subgroup of G and
Φ(G) = 1.
    Let H be a maximal subgroup of G such that N is not contained in
H and H has the largest possible order. Then CoreG (H) = 1. Let ψ be
a nonprincipal P-character of G with respect to H. If ker ψ ̸= 1, then
N ≤ ker ψ, and so ker ψ ̸≤ H. It follows that G = Hker ψ and ψH is
irreducible. Since [ψH , 1H ] = [ψ, (1H )G ] > 0, we have that ψH = 1H . In
particular, H ≤ ker ψ, a contradiction. So ker ψ ̸= 1.
    Now, by assumption, we may assume that ψ = µG , where µ is a linear
character of some subgroup H1 of G. If H1 = G, then ψ = µ is a linear con-
stituent of (1H )G , so ψH = 1H . This implies that H ≤ ker ψ, a contradiction.
So H1 < G. Since

               (1H )G (1) = |G : H| ≥ 1 + ψ(1) = 1 + |G : H1 |,

we have that |H1 | > |H|. By the choice of H,Twe get that N ≤ H1 . It follows
that 1 ̸= N = N ′ ≤ H1′ ≤ ker µ, and N ≤       (ker µ)x = ker µG = ker ψ, a
                                              x∈G
contradiction. The proof is complete. □

   For the proof of Theorem B, we need the following Lemma.

Lemma 2.1. [4, Proposition 2.3 (2)] Let G be a solvable group and G =
N ⋊ H, where H is a maximal subgroup of G and N is a minimal normal
subgroup of G. Then the map Θ : χ 7→ Irr(χN ) is a bijection of Irr(1H )G
onto the set of G-orbits of Irr(N ). Furthermore, if λ ∈ Irr(χN ), then λ is
extendible to IG (λ), and we have χ(1) = |G : IG (λ)|, where IG (λ) is the
inertia group of λ in G.

Proof of Theorem B. Suppose that H is a normal π-complement of G,
and let χ be a Pπ -character of G with respect to a maximal subgroup M .
Then |G : M | is a π-number. Since H is a normal Hall π ′ -subgroup of G, we
have that H ≤ M and G/H is a solvable π-group. By definition, since χ is
an irreducible constituent of (1M )G , it follows that χ lies over 1M and 1H lies
under χ. So H ≤ ker(χ) and χ(1) is a π-number, as desired.
    Conversely, suppose that all Pπ -character degrees of G are π-number. Let
N be a minimal normal subgroup G. By induction hypothesis, G/N has a
normal π-complement N K/N , where K is a Hall π ′ -subgroup of G. Clearly,
N is the unique minimal subgroup of G.

                                       3
      In what following, it is sufficient to show that N K has a normal Hall
π ′ -subgroup.
      Since G is π-solvable, N is a π ′ -group or elementary abelian p-group for
some prime p ∈ π. If N is a π ′ -group, then N K is a π ′ -group and N K is a
normal Hall π ′ -subgroup, as desired.
      Now suppose N is an elementary abelian p-group, where p ∈ π. If Φ(G) ̸=
1, then N ≤ Φ(G). By the Frattini argument, G = N KNG (K) = N NG (K).
Since N ≤ Φ(G), it follows that G = NG (K), so L ⊴ G, and thus L ⊴ K.
      Thus, we may assume that Φ(G) = 1, and N is not contained in Φ(G).
Choose a maximal subgroup M of G such that N ̸≤ M . Then G = N ⋊ M ,
and M is not normal in G.
      Let λ ∈ Irr(N ). By Lemma 2.1, there exists an irreducible constitu-
ent of (1M )G , say χ, such that λ is an irreducible constituent of χN , and
χ(1) = |G : IG (λ)|. By the hypothesis, χ(1) is a π-number. So we may
assume that N K ≤ T , where T = IG (λ). By Lemma 2.1 again, we see that
λ extends to Irr(T ). As a result, λ extends to some N K. By [2, Theorem
3.17], N K has a normal Hall π ′ -subgroup. □

Proof of Theorem C. We suppose that IrrP (G) = Irr(G), and we proceed
by induction on |G| to show that G must be a π-group. We can assume
that |G| > 1, and we let N be minimal normal in G. Since all members of
Irr(G/N ) are Pπ -characters, the inductive hypothesis implies that G/N is a
π-group, and thus it suffices to show that N is a π-group.
    Recall that a minimal normal subgroup of G must be either a π ′ -group or
a π-group. Let χ be a Pπ -character of G with respect to a maximal subgroup
M of G, and |G : M | be a π-number. Then M contains some Hall π ′ -group K
of G. It follows that Oπ′ (G) ≤ K ≤ M , and so Oπ′ (G) ≤ CoreG (M ) = ker χ.
    Now, if N is a π ′ -group, then N ⊆ ker(χ) for all χ ∈ IrrP (G) = Irr(G),
and since N > 1, this is a contradiction. It follows that N is a π-group, as
wanted. □
